name: Quinine skin lightener

card.summary: An antimalarial alkaloid reported in illicit lightening products, with no studies of it for skin tone.
card.note: Associated with the illegal lightening market; no efficacy or safety studies found.

quick.overview:
Quinine is mentioned as an ingredient found in some illegal skin-lightening products, alongside steroids and mercury compounds.

No studies of it as a skin lightener were found.
quick.mechanism: No mechanism for skin lightening is described in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Products in the illicit market are reported to contain hazardous ingredients such as mercury and potent steroids, and regulators in several countries have acted against them. Quinine-specific harms in this use were not documented in the sources reviewed.

lead: Quinine has been reported as an ingredient in some skin-lightening products, which people use hoping for a lighter or more even complexion. It is named among substances found in illegal lightening products alongside corticosteroids, mercury compounds and bleach-based preparations; Wikipedia's skin whitening article mentions it in connection with a 1997 Paris police crackdown on illegal trafficking of such products [1].

Quinine itself is an alkaloid from cinchona bark, used mainly as a malaria medicine and as the bitter flavouring in tonic water. It was isolated by French chemists in 1820 and is prescription-only as a drug in the US, Canada, UK and Australia [2].

No published trial has tested quinine as a skin lightener, and its mechanism in that role is not described in the sources. Wikipedia's quinine article does not mention skin lightening or hyperpigmentation [2].

chain: Quinine appears in some lightening products
Claimed lighter or more even complexion
Unverified outcome; ingredient not documented as an approved lightener
angle.text: Quinine appears in reports of illegal lightening products rather than as an established cosmetic agent. People seeking a lighter skin tone generally turn to other documented ingredients.

paras: Skin lightening products have drawn regulatory attention for ingredients including mercury, hydroquinone and potent corticosteroids. The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000, and several countries restrict mercury-containing products, though enforcement varies and such products remain sold online [1]. Quinine appears in the article only as one of the substances found in the illegal market [1].

Wikipedia notes quinine as a drug can make skin more prone to sunburn (photosensitivity) and can cause rashes, itching, hives and angioedema, with severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis reported [2]. Other documented adverse effects include cinchonism (headache, ringing in the ears, vision changes, nausea), low platelets and heart rhythm problems [2]. These relate to quinine as a medicine, not to its use in lightening creams.

timeline.event: French chemists isolate quinine from cinchona bark [2].
Paris police crack down on illegal trafficking of skin-lightening products [1].
